621: A is correct because S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically and asynchronously copies every new object from the source bucket to a destination bucket in another Region, directly meeting the need to store copies of all new photos in us-east-1 with minimal setup and no custom code. It is a native S3 feature that continuously replicates uploads once configured. The Lambda-based alternative requires developing and maintaining custom copy logic, adding operational effort.
622: A is correct because DynamoDB with on-demand capacity instantly accommodates millions of users during the 4-hour morning surge and scales back down automatically, charging only for requests actually served, while its flexible NoSQL data model lets the data architects rapidly evolve the schema. D is correct because deploying the static single page in S3 and serving it through CloudFront is the most scalable pattern for static content, since both services are fully managed and inherently elastic with no servers to administer. Aurora Serverless and DynamoDB auto scaling respond to load more gradually, and an EC2 fleet with EFS adds far more operational effort than S3 with CloudFront.
623: B is correct because AWS WAF can be attached directly to an Amazon API Gateway stage, and its managed rule groups specifically protect against SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks, which is exactly what is required. This is the most operationally efficient approach because no additional infrastructure is needed in front of API Gateway. AWS Shield only mitigates DDoS attacks, and inserting a CloudFront distribution solely to host WAF adds unnecessary overhead.
624: D is correct because SAML 2.0 federation lets users sign in with their existing Active Directory corporate credentials and receive temporary permissions from IAM roles that are mapped to their Active Directory groups. This preserves on-premises access through the same identity and avoids creating and maintaining a separate AWS identity for each user, unlike IAM users or a Cognito user pool. The mapped roles carry the appropriate policies, so access to AWS resources remains centrally controlled.
625: C is correct because a Route 53 geolocation routing policy resolves DNS based on the geographic location from which the query originates, so users are directed to the Application Load Balancer that serves the content permitted for their region, enforcing distribution rights. This is the standard mechanism for geographic content control. Geoproximity routing biases traffic toward resources based on distance rather than the user's location, and WAF options address security, not distribution rights.
626: B is correct because AWS DataSync performs online transfers to S3 and automatically validates data integrity by comparing source and destination data at the end of each transfer, ensuring the copied data is complete and accurate. DataSync is deployed as a simple agent on premises and manages the whole transfer. Snowball Edge is for offline physically shipped transfers, S3 File Gateway lacks the same automatic post-transfer integrity validation, and Transfer Acceleration only speeds uploads.
627: A is correct because Amazon Route 53 is a fully managed, highly available DNS service, so creating 200 hosted zones and importing the zone files eliminates the need to patch, scale, and maintain self-managed DNS servers. Route 53 is built to easily handle millions of queries per day across its distributed resolver infrastructure. The EC2-based options retain the operational overhead of running and recovering DNS servers.
628: C is correct because S3 Storage Lens provides organization-wide storage metrics across all accounts and Regions in AWS Organizations, and its dashboard directly reports incomplete multipart upload object counts so the company can identify cost waste for compliance reporting. It is a fully managed S3 feature requiring only enablement, with no code or infrastructure. AWS Config rules do not inspect S3 multipart upload state, SCPs enforce guardrails rather than generate reports, and Multi-Region Access Points route requests rather than report on them.
629: D is correct because RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a fully synchronized staging environment of the production database on the new MySQL version, allowing the company to test functionality against production-like data and then switch over in about a minute with no data loss or downtime. The entire workflow is managed natively by RDS, giving the least operational overhead. Snapshot, native backup, and DMS approaches involve more manual steps and slower cutover.
630: C is correct because an ECS Fargate task is serverless, so the company pays only for the roughly two hours the daily job actually runs instead of keeping capacity provisioned around the clock. Fargate also supports jobs running up to two hours, whereas a single Lambda invocation is capped at 15 minutes, and an EC2 Reserved Instance would be billed continuously for a job that needs only two hours. EC2-backed ECS additionally requires managing the underlying instances.
631: B is correct because Amazon Neptune is a managed graph database purpose-built for storing and querying highly connected data such as user profiles, relationships, and interactions, and it can power the relationship analysis behind user recommendations. Neptune Streams is a native feature that exposes changes to the graph in near real time, letting the monitoring application consume changes without extra infrastructure. Pairing Neptune with Kinesis Data Streams adds unnecessary components, and QLDB is a ledger database not designed for graph relationship queries.
632: C is correct because Amazon EFS provides a shared, POSIX-compliant file system that can be mounted concurrently by the EC2 Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones, allowing them to jointly access and modify the same data set that is analyzed hourly. EFS also grows automatically as storage needs expand over the next six months with no capacity provisioning. EBS volumes cannot be shared across instances in this way, and S3 Glacier is an archive tier unsuitable for regular modification and hourly analysis.
633: C is correct because creating an RDS read replica offloads read queries from the source Multi-AZ DB instance, directly relieving the query load that is causing the performance problems. Read replicas are purpose-built to serve read traffic and can be added as needed. The Multi-AZ standby replica is intentionally unavailable to applications, so it cannot serve reads.
634: C is correct because cross-account access uses bucket policies and IAM roles to grant each agency's own AWS account read-only access to the S3 data without copying it or exposing it publicly, keeping the data under the source account's control. This is the most secure and operationally efficient approach since the agencies use their existing identities in their own accounts. Making the bucket public or creating IAM users for external analysts in the source account violates least-privilege best practices.
635: C is correct because deploying FSx for ONTAP in the secondary Region and using NetApp SnapMirror, a built-in ONTAP replication feature, keeps the DR data accessible over the same CIFS and NFS protocols used in the primary Region, so EC2 applications in the secondary Region access data exactly as before. SnapMirror is managed within the ONTAP environment with minimal configuration, giving the least operational overhead. Backup-and-restore approaches require longer recovery time and more manual steps, and EFS does not support CIFS.
636: C is correct because subscribing an SQS queue to the SNS topic durably buffers the S3 event notifications and then triggers the Lambda function, decoupling event production from processing and letting Lambda scale reliably through bursts of file-creation events with built-in retries on failure. This SNS-to-SQS fan-out is the standard scalable serverless event-processing pattern. The container-based alternatives add orchestration complexity without benefit.
637: B is correct because AWS Lambda behind API Gateway automatically scales from zero to over 500 requests per second with no provisioning, and it costs nothing when there is no traffic, matching the sudden and unpredictable request pattern. C is correct because Amazon DynamoDB is a key-value database that handles simple key-value queries, absorbs spiky and unpredictable traffic with on-demand capacity, and scales effortlessly beyond the current 1 GB of data. Aurora and EC2 Auto Scaling options require provisioned capacity and administration the workload does not need.
638: A is correct because S3 presigned URLs grant employees secure, time-limited access to upload or download data directly from the S3 bucket, and a Lambda function can generate them on demand without creating or managing any user identities. Employees need no AWS credentials or console access, so operational overhead is minimized. Per-employee IAM users, Storage Gateway mounts, and a custom SFTP identity provider all require far more identity management effort.
639: A is correct because traffic favoring a single target is the classic symptom of sticky sessions, and disabling session affinity on the ALB allows the balancer to distribute new requests evenly across all healthy EC2 instances. This restores balanced utilization and removes the latency caused by the overloaded instance. Sticky sessions are only needed when session state must remain on one server.
640: B is correct because AWS KMS requires the key policy to grant the decrypt permission to the calling principal, and authorizing the Lambda execution role in the KMS key policy is what allows that role to decrypt with the key. E is correct because the Lambda function also needs an execution role with an IAM policy containing kms:Decrypt attached to the function, which satisfies the IAM side of the dual authorization model that KMS enforces. Lambda resource policies only control who can invoke the function rather than what the function's code may access, and IAM policies cannot be attached directly to a function.
